[
  {
    "n": 1,
    "title": "Foundations and Core Philosophy of Optimization",
    "scope": "Introduces optimization as the purposeful discipline of finding the best parameter values or system structures under constraints. Explains why optimization is studied across science, engineering, and economics beyond mere feasibility. Contrasts exact closed-form solutions with iterative, approximate algorithmic solutions, highlighting convergence rate, accuracy, and the role of heuristic search.",
    "key_points": [
      "Definition: Optimization is the process of maximizing or minimizing a mathematical objective function depending on parameters.",
      "Algorithmic nature: Operations research problems rarely yield closed-form formulas; they are solved iteratively via algorithms moving successively closer to the optimum.",
      "Algorithmic challenges: Numerical convergence speed, precision limits, computational complexity, and the necessity of computer-assisted evaluation.",
      "Heuristic fallback: When models are too complex for exact algorithms, heuristics (intelligent search rules of thumb) seek satisfactory near-optimal solutions."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 2,
    "title": "Data-Driven Optimization Motivating Examples",
    "scope": "Demonstrates how real-world problems in data analysis, machine learning, and discrete networks are cast into mathematical optimization problems. Details least-squares fitting as an overdetermined system solved via normal equations, artificial neural network training as weight and bias misfit minimization, and the traveling salesperson problem as a graph-based combinatorial path minimization.",
    "key_points": [
      "Least-Squares Data Fitting: Given points (-1, 1), (1, 1), and (2, 3), the inconsistent system Ax = b is solved via the normal equations A^T A x_hat = A^T b.",
      "Numerical least-squares solution: Matrix equation [[3, 2], [2, 6]][C; D] = [5; 6] yields best affine line C_hat + D_hat*t = 9/7 + (4/7)t, minimizing squared error via orthogonal projection.",
      "Neural Network Training: Adjusting weights w and biases b to minimize the misfit objective function f(sum_i w_i x_ik + b) - y_k across training samples, extensible to multi-layer concatenations.",
      "Traveling Salesperson Problem (TSP): Graph-based combinatorial optimization seeking a closed tour of minimal total cost/airfare visiting each node/city exactly once."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 3,
    "title": "Problem Anatomy, Decision Frameworks, and Operations Research Phases",
    "scope": "Establishes the three fundamental components of any optimization problem: decision alternatives, constraints, and the objective criterion. Analyzes a real-world multi-week business travel purchasing problem to evaluate discrete strategies. Classifies the taxonomy of Operations Research methods and defines the five formal phases of an OR project.",
    "key_points": [
      "Three model pillars: Decision alternatives (variables to choose), constraints (system restrictions), and objective criterion (evaluative metric to maximize/minimize).",
      "Kazan-Moscow travel case study: 5-week travel requiring Monday departure and Wednesday return; evaluates regular tickets ($2000), weekend-spanning roundtrips with one-way legs ($1880), and staggered weekend-spanning tickets ($1600 optimum).",
      "Definitions: Feasible solution, feasible set/space, optimal solution, infeasible problem (empty feasible set), and solvable problem (admits an optimum).",
      "Four OR method categories: Mathematical programming (calculus, LP, NLP, DP, IP), stochastic processes (Markov, queuing, reliability), statistical methods (regression, experimental design), and nontraditional techniques (genetic algorithms, simulated annealing, PSO, neural networks).",
      "Five phases of an OR study: 1. Problem definition, 2. Model construction, 3. Model solution (mathematically best-defined), 4. Model validation, and 5. Implementation."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 4,
    "title": "Mathematical Programming Formulations and Problem Taxonomies",
    "scope": "Provides the general mathematical formulation of constrained and unconstrained optimization problems. Distinguishes between continuous, discrete, and combinatorial domains, and defines convex optimization via Jensen-type inequalities. Emphasizes that optimization classification is a property of problem representation rather than reducible equivalence.",
    "key_points": [
      "General constrained problem: min f(X) subject to inequality constraints g_j(X) <= 0 (j=1,...,m), equality constraints l_j(X) = 0 (j=1,...,p), and domain X in R^n.",
      "Unconstrained problem: min f(X) with no constraints (m = p = 0).",
      "Domain dichotomy: Continuous optimization (X is R^n, box, or simplex) versus discrete/combinatorial optimization (X is integral or binary vectors).",
      "Convex optimization definition: Objective and inequality constraints satisfy g_j(alpha*x + beta*y) <= alpha*g_j(x) + beta*g_j(y) for all alpha, beta >= 0 with alpha + beta = 1.",
      "Representation criterion: Problem classes are governed by how the problem is presented (e.g., nonlinear terms like exp(x_1) or infinite constraint sets exclude a problem from linear optimization, regardless of potential transformations)."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 5,
    "title": "Linear Programming Modeling and Canonical Equivalence Transformations",
    "scope": "Formulates the rules for translating real-world production, blending, and scheduling problems into linear programs. Teaches algebraic equivalence rules to transform any general linear program into canonical maximization form. Examines classic production-mix (Tatar-Paint), dietary blending (Ozark Farms and general n-product m-nutrient diet), and equipment allocation models.",
    "key_points": [
      "LP definition: Mathematical program where the objective function and all constraint equations/inequalities are linear functions of decision variables.",
      "Standard equivalence operations: Flipping inequalities by multiplying by -1; replacing equality a^T x = b with two opposing inequalities a^T x <= b and -a^T x <= -b; converting min c^T x to max (-c)^T x.",
      "Canonical form notations: Term-wise (sum c_j x_j), constraint-wise (a_i^T x <= b_i), and matrix-vector notation (max c^T x s.t. Ax <= b).",
      "Tatar-Paint production formulation: Maximize profit z = 5x_1 + 4x_2 subject to raw material limits (6x_1 + 4x_2 <= 24, x_1 + 2x_2 <= 6), market limits (x_2 - x_1 <= 1, x_2 <= 2), and non-negativity (x_1, x_2 >= 0).",
      "Diet problem formulation: Minimize mix cost z = 0.3x_1 + 0.9x_2 subject to total bulk (x_1 + x_2 >= 800), protein bound (0.09x_1 + 0.6x_2 >= 0.3(x_1 + x_2)), fiber bound (0.02x_1 + 0.06x_2 <= 0.05(x_1 + x_2)), and non-negativity.",
      "Equipment scheduling model: Maximizing revenue over 3 products and 4 equipment types subject to total available machine hours."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 6,
    "title": "Graphical Solution Method and Geometric Outcomes in 2D",
    "scope": "Teaches the step-by-step graphical method for solving two-variable linear programs. Explains how half-spaces define a convex polygonal feasible region and how the objective function vector c defines level lines perpendicular to it. Catalogs all possible geometric solution outcomes: unique extreme-point optimum, alternative (multiple) optima along an entire boundary segment, and infeasible (empty) regions.",
    "key_points": [
      "Two-step graphical procedure: 1. Delineate the feasible solution space by intersecting constraint half-planes; 2. Determine the optimal point by sweeping level lines of the objective function across the region.",
      "Level line geometry: The objective level line c_1 x_1 + c_2 x_2 = z is orthogonal to the gradient vector c = (c_1, c_2); maximizing moves the line in the direction of c, minimizing moves opposite to c.",
      "Tatar-Paint graphical solution: Level lines sweep to the last contact point at vertex C(3, 1.5), achieving maximum profit z = 21 ($21,000).",
      "Diet minimization graphical solution: Sweeping inward reaches first contact point at intersection (470.6, 329.4) yielding minimum cost z = $437.64.",
      "Alternative/multiple optima: When the objective level line is parallel to a binding constraint boundary, all points on the segment are optimal (e.g., segment AC in Lab 1 Problem 3 with max value 8).",
      "Infeasible region: When constraints contradict each other, their intersection is empty and no feasible solution exists (Lab 1 Problem 4)."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 7,
    "title": "The Geometric-Algebraic Bridge: Slack Variables, Basic Solutions, and BFS",
    "scope": "Bridges visual geometry and multi-dimensional linear algebra. Explains why infinite feasible solution spaces can be optimized by evaluating only a finite number of corner points. Defines slack variables to transform inequalities into equations, classifies basic versus nonbasic variables, derives the combinatorial formula for candidate solutions, and maps basic feasible solutions directly to geometric vertices.",
    "key_points": [
      "Fundamental theorem insight: The feasible region contains an infinite continuum of points, but optimal solutions always occur at extreme points (vertices), enabling finite algebraic search.",
      "Augmented standard equality form: Converting m linear inequalities into equalities by adding non-negative slack variables s_i (m equations in n variables, m < n).",
      "Basic and nonbasic partition: Setting n - m variables to zero (nonbasic variables) and uniquely solving the m equations for the remaining m variables (basic variables) yields a basic solution.",
      "Combinatorial bound: The maximum number of basic solutions is given by C(n, m) = n! / (m!(n - m)!).",
      "Basic Feasible Solution (BFS): A basic solution where all basic variables satisfy non-negativity; corresponds exactly to a geometric corner point.",
      "Infeasible basic solutions: Basic solutions where one or more basic variables are negative; corresponds to intersections of constraint boundary lines lying outside the feasible region (e.g., points E and F in the 2-variable, 4-variable slack example)."
    ]
  },
  {
    "n": 8,
    "title": "The Simplex Method via Algebraic Dictionaries",
    "scope": "Develops the simplex algorithm from scratch using the dictionary representation. Details how dependent basic variables and the objective function are expressed in terms of independent nonbasic variables. Formalizes the iteration mechanics: entering variable selection, the minimum ratio test to preserve feasibility, pivot row operations, and the dictionary stopping criterion for optimality.",
    "key_points": [
      "Dictionary form: Expressing the objective z and each basic variable explicitly as linear combinations of nonbasic variables.",
      "Initial dictionary: Formed by setting decision variables as nonbasic (zero) and slack variables as basic (equaling RHS), valid when RHS >= 0.",
      "Entering variable rule: Select a nonbasic variable with a strictly positive coefficient in the z-row to increase the objective (maximization).",
      "Minimum ratio test: Increasing the entering variable decreases basic variables; non-negativity imposes upper bounds, and the tightest bound identifies the leaving variable to prevent infeasibility.",
      "Pivoting operation: Express the entering variable in terms of the leaving variable and remaining nonbasics, then substitute into all other dictionary equations and the z-row.",
      "Optimality certificate: When all nonbasic coefficients in the objective dictionary row become non-positive (<= 0), no further increase is possible and the current BFS is optimal.",
      "Step-by-step 3-variable walk-through: Progresses from initial dictionary (z = 0) via pivot on x_1 (z = 12.5) to second pivot on x_3, terminating at optimal z = 13 with solution (x_1=2, x_2=0, x_3=1, s_1=0, s_2=1, s_3=0)."
    ]
  }
]
